claims.statement: Learner-controlled pause, replay, rewind and related playback controls can support L2 comprehension repair and lower-level processing, but learners vary in how purposefully they use these controls and may need training.

Automatically repeating or slowing bounded speech segments predicted to be difficult can improve local recognition/comprehension under assisted conditions, but current evidence does not establish delayed transfer to unseen continuous speech.
Artificial pause placement changes the temporal/prosodic structure available to L2 listeners, and its processing effects can vary with pause location and learner proficiency.

In dynamic multimedia outside L2 listening, both system-determined and learner-controlled pausing can improve learning relative to uninterrupted presentation under some complexity conditions; this supports a processing-time mechanism but cannot by itself justify an L2 auto-pause policy.
Paused transcription can diagnose word-recognition and segmentation breakdowns while keeping target phrases embedded in connected discourse, making pausing useful as a diagnostic microtask.
Temporal phenomena in natural unscripted speech, including filled pauses, have context-dependent effects on L2 comprehension rather than a uniformly beneficial or harmful effect.

Adding processing time through pauses can improve comprehension in some L2 conditions, but pause benefits depend on placement, material and listener characteristics rather than following a universal frequency or duration rule.

A Vietnamese beginner EFL intervention provides population-relevant evidence that self-regulated prosody-focused listening practice can improve listening outcomes, but it does not isolate auto-pause as the causal mechanism.

Success after system-inserted pauses or segmented repair is not equivalent to success under first-seen continuous natural temporal flow because the intervention changes exposure and processing conditions.

Current evidence does not justify automatically pausing every predicted unknown word or every sentence in authentic video; such policies can introduce unnecessary interruptions and alter natural segmentation cues.

Failure-contingent temporal repair is a plausible way to preserve first-pass continuous-listening evidence while still offering replay or bounded pause support after breakdown, but comparative efficacy has not been established for Vietnamese near-A0 learners.
If automated difficulty detection triggers temporal support, detector errors create pedagogical errors: false positives interrupt learnable speech and false negatives miss repair opportunities.

The optimal pause boundary type, duration, trigger threshold and fading policy for Vietnamese near-A0 Nếp learners must be validated against delayed unseen continuous listening rather than immediate assisted comprehension alone.
